decks.title: Sulphuric Acid — Part 1: The Contact process and the dilute acid
goals: Write the equations, with catalyst and conditions, for the Contact process
Explain why sulphur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid and not in water
Explain why sulphuric acid is dibasic and forms normal and acid salts
Write equations for dilute sulphuric acid with metals, oxides, hydroxides, carbonates, hydrogen carbonates, sulphites, hydrogen sulphites and sulphides

slides.heading: The king of chemicals
slides.body_md: Part 1 — Sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄, is called the **king of chemicals**: more of it is made than any other chemical, for **fertilisers**, **detergents**, **paints**, **car batteries** and the refining of petroleum.

rows: Gives out a lot of heat

visual.alt: Table of the formula, appearance, boiling point and uses of sulphuric acid

slides.narration: Namaste! Sulphuric acid is often called the king of chemicals, because industry makes more of it than of any other chemical. It goes into fertilisers, detergents, paints and car batteries. It is a heavy, oily, colourless liquid with a high boiling point. In this part we see how it is manufactured and how the dilute acid behaves.

slides.heading: Contact process, step 1: sulphur dioxide
slides.body_md: Sulphur is **burnt in air** to give sulphur dioxide. (Sulphur dioxide can also be obtained by **roasting iron pyrites**, FeS₂.) The gas is **purified and dried** before the next step.

visual.alt: Equation: sulphur plus oxygen gives sulphur dioxide
visual.caption: Burning sulphur in air

slides.narration: The Contact process starts with sulphur dioxide. Molten sulphur is burnt in air, and it combines with oxygen to form sulphur dioxide gas. Sulphur dioxide can also come from roasting iron pyrites, an ore of iron and sulphur. Before going further, the gas is cleaned and dried.

slides.heading: Contact process, step 2: the catalytic step
slides.body_md: Sulphur dioxide and **excess air** pass over **vanadium pentoxide** (V₂O₅) at about **450 °C** and **1–2 atm**. The reaction is **reversible** and **exothermic**. The name “contact” comes from the gases reacting **in contact with the catalyst** surface.

visual.alt: Equation: two sulphur dioxide plus oxygen reversibly gives two sulphur trioxide
visual.caption: Vanadium pentoxide, about 450 °C, 1–2 atm

slides.narration: This is the key step. Sulphur dioxide and extra air are passed over a catalyst of vanadium pentoxide at about four hundred and fifty degrees Celsius and only one or two atmospheres. Sulphur dioxide combines with oxygen to form sulphur trioxide. The reaction is reversible and gives out heat, and it takes place on the surface of the catalyst, which gives the process its name.

slides.heading: Quick check: the catalyst
slides.body_md: Recall the catalyst and temperature for oxidising sulphur dioxide.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which oxide of vanadium is used, and at about what temperature?

slides.heading: Contact process: the whole route
slides.body_md:
**Step 3.** Sulphur trioxide is **dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid** to give **oleum** (fuming sulphuric acid).

**Step 4.** Oleum is **diluted with the right amount of water** to give sulphuric acid of the required strength.

SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇; H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄

visual.alt: Flow of the Contact process from sulphur and air through sulphur dioxide, sulphur trioxide and oleum to sulphuric acid

slides.narration: Here is the full route. Sulphur burns to sulphur dioxide, which is oxidised to sulphur trioxide over the catalyst. The sulphur trioxide is then dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid, forming a thick, fuming liquid called oleum. Finally, oleum is diluted with exactly the right amount of water to give sulphuric acid.

slides.heading: Why not dissolve SO₃ in water?
slides.body_md: Sulphur trioxide reacts with water **very exothermically**. The heat turns the acid into a **dense fog (mist)** of tiny droplets that does **not condense easily** and escapes. Dissolving it in **concentrated sulphuric acid** is smooth and controllable.

rows: Violent, heat given out; acid mist forms and is lost

visual.alt: Table comparing absorption of sulphur trioxide in water and in concentrated sulphuric acid

slides.narration: Why the extra step? If sulphur trioxide is passed straight into water, the reaction is so violent and gives out so much heat that a thick fog of acid droplets forms. This fog is very hard to condense, so acid is lost into the air. Absorbing the gas in concentrated sulphuric acid avoids the fog, and the oleum can then be diluted safely.

slides.heading: Worked example: acid from sulphur
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What mass of sulphuric acid can be made from 8 g of sulphur in the Contact process, assuming complete conversion? (S = 32, H = 1, O = 16)

**Step 1.** Follow the sulphur: S → SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄, so 1 mole S gives 1 mole H₂SO₄.

**Step 2.** Moles of S = 8 ÷ 32 = 0.25.

**Step 3.** H₂SO₄ = 2 + 32 + 64 = 98; mass = 0.25 × 98 = **24.5 g**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from 8 grams of sulphur to 24.5 grams of sulphuric acid

slides.narration: Track the sulphur atom through every step: one sulphur atom ends up in one sulphuric acid molecule. Eight grams of sulphur is a quarter of a mole, because the molar mass of sulphur is thirty two. A quarter of a mole of sulphuric acid, with molar mass ninety eight, weighs twenty four point five grams.

slides.body_md: Explain why sulphur trioxide is not passed directly into water.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the heat given out and what happens to the acid formed.

slides.heading: A dibasic acid
slides.body_md:
Each molecule of sulphuric acid can give **two hydrogen ions**, so it is **dibasic**: H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻ (in two stages, through HSO₄⁻). It therefore forms **two kinds of salt** with a base:

- an **acid salt** when only one H is replaced: NaOH + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + H₂O
- a **normal salt** when both are replaced: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O

headers: Moles of NaOH per mole of H₂SO₄

visual.alt: Table of the acid salt and the normal salt formed from sulphuric acid and sodium hydroxide

slides.narration: Every sulphuric acid molecule has two hydrogen atoms that can be replaced by a metal, so we call it dibasic. If only one of them is replaced, we get an acid salt such as sodium hydrogen sulphate, which still has a replaceable hydrogen. If both are replaced, we get a normal salt, sodium sulphate. Which one forms depends on how much alkali is used.

slides.heading: Dilute acid with metals, oxides and hydroxides
slides.body_md: Dilute sulphuric acid behaves as a typical **strong acid**. Metals **above hydrogen** give **hydrogen**; copper does not react.

visual.alt: Table of dilute sulphuric acid with metals, a basic oxide and hydroxides

slides.narration: Dilute sulphuric acid is a strong acid. Magnesium and iron, which are above hydrogen in the activity series, dissolve in it and give hydrogen gas and the metal sulphate. Copper, below hydrogen, does not react. Basic oxides such as black copper oxide dissolve to give a sulphate and water, and alkalis are neutralised in the same way.

slides.heading: Dilute acid with salts of weaker acids
slides.body_md: Dilute sulphuric acid **displaces weaker, more volatile acids** from their salts, which then give off a gas:

visual.alt: Table of dilute sulphuric acid with a carbonate, a hydrogen carbonate, a sulphite, a hydrogen sulphite and a sulphide

slides.narration: Salts of weaker acids react with dilute sulphuric acid and give off a gas. Carbonates and hydrogen carbonates give carbon dioxide. Sulphites and hydrogen sulphites give sulphur dioxide, which smells of burning sulphur. Sulphides give hydrogen sulphide, with its smell of rotten eggs. In every case a sulphate is left behind.

slides.heading: Worked example: the reaction that stops
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Marble chips (calcium carbonate) are dropped into dilute sulphuric acid. There is brisk fizzing at first, but it soon stops although both marble and acid are left. Explain, with an equation.

**Step 1.** CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂.

**Step 2.** Calcium sulphate is **only slightly soluble**. It forms a **coating** on the marble.

**Step 3.** The coating **stops the acid reaching** the carbonate, so the reaction stops. (Dilute hydrochloric acid is used instead to make CO₂.)

visual.alt: Table comparing marble chips with dilute sulphuric acid and dilute hydrochloric acid

slides.narration: At first marble fizzes in dilute sulphuric acid as carbon dioxide is given off. But the calcium sulphate formed hardly dissolves, so it builds up as a coat over the chips. The acid can no longer reach the calcium carbonate underneath, and the fizzing stops. That is why dilute hydrochloric acid, not sulphuric acid, is used with marble to prepare carbon dioxide.

slides.heading: Quick check: normal or acid salt?
slides.body_md: Decide which salt forms when sodium hydroxide and sulphuric acid react in a one to one mole ratio.
slides.narration: Quick check. If only one of the two hydrogens is replaced, what kind of salt do you get?

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Contact: S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅, about 450 °C, 1–2 atm); SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇; H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.
SO₃ is not absorbed in water: a dense acid mist forms.
Dibasic: acid salts (NaHSO₄) and normal salts (Na₂SO₄).
Dilute acid: metals above H give H₂; carbonates give CO₂; sulphites give SO₂; sulphides give H₂S.

visual.alt: Summary table of the four steps of the Contact process with conditions

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. In the Contact process, sulphur burns to sulphur dioxide, which is oxidised over vanadium pentoxide to sulphur trioxide. This is absorbed in concentrated acid to give oleum, which is diluted to sulphuric acid. The acid is dibasic, forming acid salts and normal salts, and the dilute acid reacts with metals, bases and salts of weaker acids.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the double arrow for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ and give catalyst, temperature and pressure.
Give the reason for oleum in one line: a dense mist of acid that does not condense.
Name the salt type: NaHSO₄ is an acid salt, Na₂SO₄ a normal salt.
Plant details are not needed: equations with conditions are enough.

rows: Vanadium pentoxide (platinum is for Ostwald’s process)
SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ in the plant
SO₃ is absorbed in conc. H₂SO₄ first
Copper does not react with the dilute acid

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Show the oxidation of sulphur dioxide with a double arrow, and always give the catalyst, temperature and pressure. Explain the use of oleum by mentioning the acid mist. Say whether a salt is an acid salt or a normal salt. And remember that copper does not react with dilute sulphuric acid.

decks.title: Sulphuric Acid — Part 2: The concentrated acid and tests
goals: Write equations for hot concentrated sulphuric acid oxidising carbon and sulphur
Describe and explain the action of concentrated sulphuric acid on sugar and on blue vitriol
Use the non-volatile nature of sulphuric acid to prepare HCl and HNO₃, and test for sulphuric acid and sulphates

slides.heading: Three powers of the concentrated acid
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **Concentrated** sulphuric acid shows three special properties besides being an acid:

rows: Drives out HCl and HNO₃ from their salts

visual.alt: Table of three properties of concentrated sulphuric acid with what each does and an example

slides.narration: Concentrated sulphuric acid is far more than a strong acid. When hot, it is an oxidising agent. It has such a strong pull on water that it removes water even from compounds like sugar. And because it has a high boiling point, it can push more volatile acids out of their salts. We look at each of these in turn.

slides.heading: Oxidising agent: carbon and sulphur
slides.body_md: **Hot concentrated** sulphuric acid gives oxygen (H₂SO₄ → H₂O + SO₂ + [O]) and is itself reduced to **sulphur dioxide**:

visual.alt: Table of the oxidation of carbon and sulphur by hot concentrated sulphuric acid

slides.narration: When it is hot and concentrated, sulphuric acid releases oxygen and is reduced to sulphur dioxide. Charcoal is oxidised to carbon dioxide, so the gas given off is a mixture of carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide. Sulphur is oxidised to sulphur dioxide, so in that case sulphur dioxide is the only gas, along with water.

slides.heading: Worked example: gas from charcoal
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 1.2 g of charcoal is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid. Find the total volume of gas (CO₂ and SO₂) at STP. (C = 12; molar volume 22.4 L)

**Step 1.** C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 2SO₂: 1 mole C gives 1 mole CO₂ and 2 moles SO₂.

**Step 2.** Moles of C = 1.2 ÷ 12 = 0.1.

**Step 3.** Gas = 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3 mole; volume = 0.3 × 22.4 = **6.72 L** (2.24 L CO₂, 4.48 L SO₂).

visual.alt: Table of the moles and volumes of carbon dioxide and sulphur dioxide from 1.2 grams of charcoal

slides.narration: The equation tells us that one unit of carbon gives one unit of carbon dioxide and two of sulphur dioxide. One point two grams of carbon is zero point one mole. So we get zero point one mole of carbon dioxide and zero point two mole of sulphur dioxide, zero point three mole in all, which is six point seven two litres at standard conditions.

slides.heading: Quick check: oxidising carbon
slides.body_md: Name the gases given off when charcoal is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid.
slides.narration: Quick check. Carbon is oxidised, and the acid is reduced. What does each become?

slides.heading: Dehydrating agent: sugar
slides.body_md:
Concentrated sulphuric acid removes **hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1** (the elements of water) from sugar. The sugar turns **yellow, brown, then black**; a **spongy column of carbon** rises, with **steam** and much **heat**. This is called **charring**.

C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O (conc. H₂SO₄)

slides.narration: Pour a little concentrated sulphuric acid onto white sugar in a beaker and wait. The sugar turns yellow, then brown, then black, and a black spongy column of carbon slowly climbs out of the beaker, hissing steam. The beaker gets very hot. The acid has pulled hydrogen and oxygen out of the sugar as water, leaving carbon behind.

slides.narration: Blue copper sulphate crystals owe their colour to water of crystallisation. When concentrated sulphuric acid is added, it takes this water away, and the blue crystals crumble to a white powder of anhydrous copper sulphate. Adding water to the white powder would bring the blue colour back.

slides.heading: Dehydration is not drying
slides.body_md: **Drying:** removing **moisture** (water that is merely present) from a substance, for example drying a gas. **Dehydration:** removing the **elements of water** (H and O in the ratio 2 : 1) from a **compound**, or its water of crystallisation.

rows: Elements of water from a compound
Moist chlorine passed through conc. H₂SO₄
Conc. H₂SO₄ on sugar or blue vitriol

visual.alt: Table comparing drying and dehydration with examples

slides.narration: Drying and dehydration are different. Drying removes water that is simply mixed with a substance, such as moisture in a gas, and the substance itself does not change. Dehydration removes hydrogen and oxygen from inside a compound, in the same ratio as in water, so a new substance forms. Charring sugar is dehydration; passing moist chlorine through the acid is drying.

slides.heading: Quick check: dehydrating sugar
slides.body_md: Name the property shown when concentrated sulphuric acid chars sugar.
slides.narration: Quick check. The acid removed hydrogen and oxygen from the sugar in the same ratio as in water. What property is that?

slides.heading: Which gases can it dry?
slides.body_md: Concentrated sulphuric acid dries gases that **do not react** with it, such as **chlorine, sulphur dioxide, hydrogen chloride, oxygen and carbon dioxide**. It **cannot dry ammonia** (a base: forms ammonium sulphate) or **hydrogen sulphide** (oxidised to sulphur).

visual.alt: Table of gases that can and cannot be dried by concentrated sulphuric acid

slides.narration: Because it absorbs water so strongly, concentrated sulphuric acid is used to dry many gases, such as chlorine, sulphur dioxide, hydrogen chloride and carbon dioxide, which simply bubble through it. But it cannot dry ammonia, which is a base and reacts with the acid, or hydrogen sulphide, which the acid oxidises to sulphur.

slides.heading: Non-volatile acid
slides.body_md:
Concentrated sulphuric acid has a **high boiling point** (about 338 °C), so it is **non-volatile**. Heated with salts of **volatile acids**, it drives those acids out as vapour, which is used to **prepare HCl and HNO₃**:

- NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl (below 200 °C)
- KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃ (below 200 °C)

visual.alt: Equation: potassium chloride plus sulphuric acid gives potassium hydrogen sulphate plus hydrogen chloride
visual.caption: Non-volatile acid driving out a volatile acid

slides.narration: Sulphuric acid boils at a much higher temperature than hydrochloric or nitric acid. So when it is heated with a chloride or a nitrate, the more volatile acid escapes as a vapour and the sulphuric acid stays behind. That is how hydrogen chloride and nitric acid are prepared in the laboratory, from common salt and from potassium nitrate.

slides.heading: Worked example: identifying a sulphate
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A colourless solution Y gives a **white precipitate** with barium chloride solution. The precipitate does **not dissolve** in dilute hydrochloric acid. Y also turns blue litmus red. Identify Y and write the equation.

**Step 1.** White precipitate with BaCl₂, insoluble in HCl → **sulphate ion** (BaSO₄).

**Step 2.** Turns blue litmus red → an **acid**.

**Step 3.** Y is **dilute sulphuric acid**: BaCl₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2HCl.

visual.alt: Table of tests on solution Y with observations and inferences

slides.narration: Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with sulphates, but also with sulphites and carbonates. Adding dilute hydrochloric acid settles it: barium sulphite and carbonate dissolve, while barium sulphate does not. Since Y also turns blue litmus red, it must be dilute sulphuric acid.

slides.heading: Tests for sulphuric acid
slides.body_md:
- **Barium chloride** (or barium nitrate) solution: **white precipitate** of BaSO₄, **insoluble** in dilute HCl or HNO₃.
- **Lead nitrate** solution: **white precipitate** of PbSO₄: Pb(NO₃)₂ + H₂SO₄ → PbSO₄ + 2HNO₃.
- **Concentrated** acid: **chars** sugar or paper.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the barium chloride test for sulphuric acid and sulphates

slides.narration: To confirm sulphuric acid, add barium chloride solution: a white precipitate of barium sulphate forms, and it does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid. Lead nitrate solution also gives a white precipitate, of lead sulphate. And a drop of the concentrated acid on sugar or paper turns it black.

visual.alt: Summary table of the properties of concentrated sulphuric acid with a key reaction for each

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Hot concentrated sulphuric acid oxidises carbon and sulphur and is reduced to sulphur dioxide. It dehydrates sugar to carbon and blue vitriol to a white powder. It dries gases that do not react with it. Its high boiling point lets it drive hydrochloric and nitric acids out of their salts. Barium chloride gives a white precipitate that confirms a sulphate.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 2

In sugar questions, give at least two observations: blackening, a rising spongy mass, steam, heat.
For drying versus dehydration, give one example of each.
In the sulphate test, always add dilute HCl to show the precipitate is insoluble.

Give an example each of drying and dehydration. And in the sulphate test, add dilute hydrochloric acid to show the white precipitate does not dissolve.

sections.heading: 1. The Contact process (equations and conditions)
sections.body_md:
- **Step 1:** sulphur burnt in air (or iron pyrites roasted) → SO₂, which is purified and dried.
- **Step 2 (contact step):** SO₂ + excess air over **vanadium pentoxide, V₂O₅**, at about **450 °C** and **1–2 atm**; reversible and exothermic.
- **Step 3:** SO₃ absorbed in **concentrated H₂SO₄** → **oleum** (fuming sulphuric acid, H₂S₂O₇).
- **Step 4:** oleum diluted with the calculated amount of water → H₂SO₄.

**Why not water?** SO₃ + H₂O is violently exothermic and forms a **dense mist** of acid droplets that does not condense easily.

key_terms.definition_md: The industrial manufacture of sulphuric acid in which sulphur dioxide and oxygen combine on the surface of a vanadium pentoxide catalyst.
H₂S₂O₇, fuming sulphuric acid, formed when sulphur trioxide dissolves in concentrated sulphuric acid.

visual.alt: Table of the conditions for the later steps of the Contact process

sections.heading: 2. Dilute sulphuric acid: a dibasic acid
sections.body_md:
Each molecule gives **two H⁺ ions** (H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻), so the acid is **dibasic** and forms **two series of salts**:

- **acid salts** (one H replaced): NaHSO₄, KHSO₄
- **normal salts** (both H replaced): Na₂SO₄, K₂SO₄

key_terms.definition_md: An acid with two replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule, which forms both acid salts and normal salts.
A salt in which only part of the replaceable hydrogen of the acid has been replaced by a metal, such as NaHSO₄.

visual.alt: Table of the salts formed by sodium hydroxide and sulphuric acid in two mole ratios

sections.heading: 3. Reactions of the dilute acid
sections.body_md:
- **Active metals** (above H): sulphate + **hydrogen**. Copper does not react.
- **Basic oxides and hydroxides:** sulphate + water.
- **Carbonates, hydrogen carbonates:** sulphate + water + **CO₂**. With marble chips the reaction soon stops: insoluble **CaSO₄** coats the chips.
- **Sulphites, hydrogen sulphites:** sulphate + water + **SO₂**.
- **Sulphides:** sulphate + **H₂S** (rotten-egg smell).

key_terms.definition_md: A strong acid reacting with a salt of a weaker or more volatile acid, setting that acid (or its gas) free.

visual.alt: Table of the gases given by salts with dilute sulphuric acid and tests for them

sections.heading: 4. Concentrated acid as an oxidising agent
sections.body_md:
**Hot concentrated** sulphuric acid gives oxygen (H₂SO₄ → H₂O + SO₂ + [O]) and is reduced to **sulphur dioxide**.

- **Carbon** is oxidised to CO₂ (gas mixture of CO₂ and SO₂).
- **Sulphur** is oxidised to SO₂ (the only gas).

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that supplies oxygen to another substance and is itself reduced.

visual.alt: Table of the gases given off when carbon and sulphur are oxidised by hot concentrated sulphuric acid

sections.heading: 5. Concentrated acid as a dehydrating agent
sections.body_md:
Concentrated sulphuric acid has a very strong attraction for water.

- **Sugar:** turns yellow → brown → black; a **black spongy mass of carbon** rises; steam; much heat (**charring**): C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O.
- **Blue vitriol:** blue crystals turn **white** as the water of crystallisation is removed: CuSO₄·5H₂O → CuSO₄ + 5H₂O.

**Drying** removes moisture that is merely present (e.g. moist Cl₂, SO₂, HCl passed through the acid); **dehydration** removes the elements of water from a compound. The acid **cannot dry NH₃** (reacts: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄) or **H₂S** (oxidised to sulphur).

key_terms.definition_md: Removal of hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio 2 : 1 (the elements of water) from a compound, or of its water of crystallisation.
Removal of moisture that is simply present in a substance, without changing the substance.

sections.heading: 6. Non-volatile nature and tests
sections.body_md:
With a boiling point of about 338 °C, sulphuric acid is **non-volatile**. Heated with salts of **volatile acids**, it drives them out: this is how **HCl** and **HNO₃** are prepared.

**Tests for sulphuric acid / a sulphate:**
- **Barium chloride** solution → **white precipitate** of BaSO₄, **insoluble in dilute HCl** (or HNO₃).
- **Lead nitrate** solution → white precipitate of PbSO₄.
- The **concentrated** acid chars sugar, wood or paper.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Using platinum (Ostwald) instead of vanadium pentoxide as the Contact catalyst.
- Writing SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ as the plant step (SO₃ is absorbed in conc. H₂SO₄ first).
- Calling the charring of sugar “oxidation” or “drying” (it is dehydration).
- Forgetting to add dilute HCl in the barium chloride test.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Contact process (1 mark per step): equation plus catalyst, temperature and pressure.
- Observations (1 mark each): colour change and the gas or residue.
- Drying versus dehydration (2 marks): one example of each.

questions.stem_md: What mass of sulphuric acid, in grams, can be made from 16 g of sulphur by the Contact process, assuming complete conversion? (S = 32, H = 1, O = 16)
questions.solution_md: Every sulphur atom ends up in one molecule of sulphuric acid ($\ce{S -> SO2 -> SO3 -> H2SO4}$), so one mole of sulphur gives one mole of acid. Moles of S $= \dfrac{16}{32} = 0.5$. Molar mass of $\ce{H2SO4} = 2 \times 1 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 98$. Mass of acid $= 0.5 \times 98 = 49$, so 49 g.

Instead it is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum (SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇), which is diluted with the right amount of water (H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄).

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the balanced equations for (i) the burning of sulphur and (ii) the catalytic oxidation of sulphur dioxide, stating the catalyst and temperature for (ii). [2]

(b) The oxidation of sulphur dioxide is reversible and exothermic. Why is excess air used, and why is the pressure only 1–2 atm? [2]

(c) (i) Why is sulphur trioxide not absorbed directly in water? (ii) Write the equation for the formation of oleum. (iii) Write the equation for the conversion of oleum into sulphuric acid. [3]

(d) 12.8 g of sulphur is completely converted into sulphuric acid. Calculate (i) the mass of sulphuric acid formed and (ii) the total volume of oxygen at STP used in the first two steps. (S = 32, H = 1, O = 16; molar volume 22.4 L) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) S + O₂ → SO₂. (ii) 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃; vanadium pentoxide, about 450 °C.

(b) Excess oxygen pushes the reversible reaction forward, converting more SO₂ to SO₃. A good conversion is already obtained at 1–2 atm, so costly high pressure is not needed.

(c) (i) The reaction is violently exothermic and forms a dense acid mist that does not condense easily. (ii) SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇. (iii) H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄.

(d) Moles of sulphur $= \dfrac{12.8}{32} = 0.4$. (i) One mole of sulphur gives one mole of sulphuric acid: mass $= 0.4 \times 98 = 39.2$, that is 39.2 g. (ii) Step 1 uses one mole of oxygen per mole of sulphur and step 2 half a mole more, so moles of oxygen $= 0.4 \times 1.5 = 0.6$; volume $= 0.6 \times 22.4 = 13.44$, that is 13.44 L.

questions.solution_md: Equations with conditions; reasons; oleum route; 1 : 1 and 1 : 1.5 ratios.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by a dibasic acid? Write the equation for the complete ionisation of sulphuric acid in water. [2]

(b) Write the balanced equations for the reaction of sodium hydroxide with sulphuric acid to form (i) an acid salt and (ii) a normal salt. [2]

(c) Write the balanced equations for dilute sulphuric acid with (i) sodium carbonate, (ii) sodium hydrogen sulphite and (iii) sodium sulphide. [3]

(d) (i) Explain why dilute sulphuric acid is not used with marble chips to prepare carbon dioxide. (ii) Calculate the mass of sodium hydroxide needed to neutralise 4.9 g of sulphuric acid completely. (Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1, S = 32) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) An acid with two replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule. H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻.

(b) (i) NaOH + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + H₂O. (ii) 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

(c) (i) Na₂CO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. (ii) 2NaHSO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O + 2SO₂. (iii) Na₂S + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂S.

(d) (i) Calcium sulphate formed is only slightly soluble; it coats the marble chips and stops the reaction. (ii) Complete neutralisation: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Moles of acid $= \dfrac{4.9}{98} = 0.05$; moles of NaOH $= 2 \times 0.05 = 0.1$; mass $= 0.1 \times 40 = 4$, that is 4 g.

questions.solution_md: Basicity; two salts; three equations; coating; 1 : 2 ratio.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the balanced equations for the action of hot concentrated sulphuric acid on (i) carbon and (ii) sulphur. [2]

(b) Concentrated sulphuric acid is added to cane sugar. State two observations and write the balanced equation. [2]

(c) (i) What is seen when concentrated sulphuric acid is added to blue vitriol? (ii) Is this drying or dehydration? Give a reason. (iii) Name one gas that concentrated sulphuric acid can dry and one it cannot. [3]

(d) 34.2 g of cane sugar (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) is completely charred by concentrated sulphuric acid. Calculate the mass of (i) carbon and (ii) water formed. (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) C + 2H₂SO₄ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 2SO₂. (ii) S + 2H₂SO₄ → 3SO₂ + 2H₂O.

(b) The sugar turns black and a black spongy mass rises out of the beaker; steam is given off and the beaker becomes hot. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ → 12C + 11H₂O.

(c) (i) The blue crystals turn white. (ii) Dehydration: the water of crystallisation is removed and a new substance, anhydrous copper(II) sulphate, forms. (iii) Can dry: chlorine (or SO₂, HCl, CO₂). Cannot dry: ammonia (or hydrogen sulphide).

(d) Molar mass of sugar $= 12 \times 12 + 22 \times 1 + 11 \times 16 = 342$. Moles $= \dfrac{34.2}{342} = 0.1$. (i) Mass of carbon $= 0.1 \times 12 \times 12 = 14.4$, that is 14.4 g. (ii) Mass of water $= 0.1 \times 11 \times 18 = 19.8$, that is 19.8 g.

questions.solution_md: Oxidation equations; charring; dehydration of blue vitriol; 1 : 12 : 11 mole ratio.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by saying that sulphuric acid is non-volatile? Write the balanced equation for its action on potassium nitrate below 200 °C. [2]

(b) Write the balanced equation for the action of concentrated sulphuric acid on sodium chloride, and explain why the concentrated acid, not the dilute acid, is used. [2]

(c) Describe a test that shows that a solution contains sulphate ions: name the reagent, state the observation and write the balanced equation for sodium sulphate. [3]

(d) Excess barium chloride solution is added to a solution of 7.1 g of sodium sulphate. Calculate the mass of barium sulphate formed. (Na = 23, S = 32, O = 16, Ba = 137) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It has a high boiling point (about 338 °C) and does not readily form vapour. KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃.

(b) NaCl + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HCl. The concentrated acid supplies little water, so the hydrogen chloride escapes as a gas instead of staying dissolved.

(c) Add barium chloride solution: a white precipitate forms that does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid. Na₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄ + 2NaCl.

(d) Molar mass of sodium sulphate $= 2 \times 23 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 142$. Moles $= \dfrac{7.1}{142} = 0.05$. One mole gives one mole of barium sulphate, molar mass $137 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 233$. Mass $= 0.05 \times 233 = 11.65$, that is 11.65 g.

questions.solution_md: Non-volatile; HCl preparation; barium chloride test; 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.stem_md:
Three colourless liquids, X, Y and Z, are concentrated sulphuric acid, dilute sulphuric acid and dilute hydrochloric acid, in some order.

(a) A drop of X on a sugar crystal turns it black. Identify X and name the property shown. Why would X not be used to dry ammonia? [3]

(b) Barium chloride solution gives a white precipitate with Y but not with Z. Identify Y and Z, and write the balanced equation for the reaction of Y. [3]

(c) (i) Y is added to sodium sulphite. Write the balanced equation and name the gas. (ii) X is heated with sulphur. Write the balanced equation. (iii) Z is added to marble chips and keeps fizzing, whereas Y soon stops. Explain. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) X is concentrated sulphuric acid; dehydrating property. Ammonia is a base and reacts with it: 2NH₃ + H₂SO₄ → (NH₄)₂SO₄.

(b) Y is dilute sulphuric acid and Z is dilute hydrochloric acid. BaCl₂ + H₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ + 2HCl.

(c) (i) Na₂SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + SO₂; sulphur dioxide. (ii) S + 2H₂SO₄ → 3SO₂ + 2H₂O. (iii) With hydrochloric acid the calcium chloride formed is very soluble, so the acid keeps reaching the marble. With sulphuric acid, slightly soluble calcium sulphate coats the chips and stops the reaction.

questions.solution_md: Charring identifies X; the sulphate test separates Y and Z; reactions and the marble difference.
